SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-1
Section 1 – Executive Summary 
1. Brief description of the PSPS event starting from the time when the utility’s Emergency
Operation Center is activated until service to all customers have been restored.
The November 24th-26th Santa Ana event transpired from a cutoff low system which
approached the coast of Southern California during the beginning of that week. Forecast
model guidance during the prior week indicated that as the system moved eastward across the
SDG&E service territory, the cutoff low would merge with another weather system (trough),
leading to an area of high northeasterly winds aloft over San Diego County. Given that a very
dry airmass (with single digit relative humidity values) was in place in conjunction with
anticipated winds across the higher terrain, a PSPS Watch was issued on Monday (11/22) and
was upgraded to a PSPS Warning on Tuesday (11/23).
The National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning for: San Diego County Mountains
and Valleys (Zone 250 & 258) from Thursday 4 AM to Friday 6 PM, Inland Orange County
(Zone 554) from Wednesday 10 AM to Friday 6 PM, Coastal Orange County (Zone 552)
from Wednesday 6 PM to Thursday 3 PM. The Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index (SAWTI)
was listed as ‘Moderate’ for Thursday and ‘Marginal’ for Wednesday (11/23) and Friday
(11/26). The Fire Potential Index (FPI) was ‘Elevated’ for all districts stating on
Thanksgiving Day (11/25) through Saturday (11/27).
On Monday, (11/22) SDG&E activated the Notification Group to initiate public safety
partner notifications.  Notifications continued Tuesday (11/23) through EOC activation.
The PSPS and EOC activation began Wednesday evening at 6 PM (11/24) and lasted until all
service to customers was restored late Friday afternoon (11/26 4:37 PM). SDG&E
deactivated its EOC on Friday afternoon at 4:53 PM (11/26).  Maximum wind gusts were
forecast to range between 30-45 mph with locally higher gusts in the most wind-prone
locations. The peak winds occurred during the pre-dawn hours of Thanksgiving Day with a
gradual diminishment during the morning hours on 11/26.

2. Decision criteria and detailed thresholds leading to de-energization including the latest
forecasted weather parameters versus actual weather. Also include a PSPS decision-
making diagram(s)/flowchart(s) or equivalent along with narrative description
SDG&E utilizes multiple factors outside of weather to assist in the decision making. Some of 
those factors pertain to information in the field based on known compliance issues on the 
electrical system, active temporary construction/configuration of the electrical system and a 
circuit risk index to identify locations in the system with a potential of having higher failure 
rates.  These factors are compiled and populated for each sectionalizing device to assist with 
developing alert speeds and increased awareness of risky assets on the electrical system.

Figure 1: PSPS Decision-Making Framework 
Sectionalizing device alert speeds are determined separately for each device tied to a weather 
station and are based on a variety of factors, such as wind speeds, vegetation risk index and 
circuit risk index.  Alert speed thresholds are lowered if Vegetation Risk Index (VRI) or 
Circuit Risk Index (CRI) is high, as seen in the figure below.  Other factors such as 
maintenance issues, existing construction, other real time observations, ongoing fires and/or 
ignitions, suppression capabilities or system protection could lower the thresholds for 
specific events.

Figure 2: Alert Speed Calculation 
SDG&E’s Fire Science and Climate Adaptation team closely monitored weather forecasts in 
advance of the approaching Santa Ana wind event and presented the latest forecast and fire 
potential information to the SDG&E Officer in Charge, who made the decision to initiate 
PSPS protocols on Monday, November 22nd for a potential PSPS event on Thursday, 
November 25th.  The factors considered when initiating the PSPS event with 72 hours’ notice 
included: 
Fire Potential Index (FPI): The FPI issued Monday morning, November 22nd at 6am 
increased the rating to “14” for Thanksgiving Day.  The increased rating was in part due to a 
combination of strong gusty winds and dry fuels that were expected across the region.  A 
rating of “14” is an indication that there could be large and damaging fires, should an ignition 
occur.  The FPI rating maintained its rating of 14 through the event and this served as a factor 
when determining PSPS. The table below illustrates the seven-day FPI forecast issued on 
Monday morning, November 22nd.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-6
Figure 3: Seven Day FPI Outlook 
SDG&E Weather Forecast:  A detailed, AI driven weather forecast was generating forecast 
by Monday morning that were consistent with what our meteorology team was forecasting, 
which was gusts 40-60 mph across the backcountry of San Diego with locally higher gusts.  
These weather forecast remain available at the San Diego Supercomputing Center at the 
following link: https://sdge.sdsc.edu/data/sdge/gust_forecast/  
Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index (SAWTI): The SAWTI that was issued on Monday 
morning from the Predictive Services unit from the Forest Service was indicating that there 
was a Moderate rating for San Diego on Wednesday, meaning that “upon ignitions, fires will 
grow rapidly and will be difficult to control”.  Additionally, this Predictive Services unit also 
designated Thursday as a “High Risk” day for large fires across southern California.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021

Figure 4: SAWTI 
National Weather Service (NWS) Forecast: The NWS was forecasting the potential for 
Santa Ana winds in their forecast close to a week in advance, though it was late in the 
weekend (~11/21) when it became apparent that the potential for rainfall in the days ahead of 
Thanksgiving was looking less likely, and the potential for critical fire danger started to be 
mentioned by the NWS.  This eventually led to an issuance of a Fire Weather Watch and Red 
Flag Warning as the event approached.  There was also a designation of Critical Fire Weather 
from the NWS Storm Prediction Center.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-8
Figure 5: NWS Forecast 
Wildfire vs PSPS Risk Forecast: In advance of the approaching Santa Ana Wind event, 
wildfire risk modeling was conducted to determine if this preliminary modeling was 
indicating that there were areas in the SDG&E service territory where the wildfire risk could 
outweigh the risk of PSPS.  The modeling did show that this was possible during the event, 
and this was reported to operational leadership and leveraged as a factor in the decision to 
initiate PSPS protocols. 
3. A thorough and detailed description of the quantitative and qualitative factors it
considered in calling, sustaining, or curtailing each de-energization event including any
fire risk or PSPS risk modeling results and information regarding why the de-
energization event was a last resort, and a specification of the factors that led to the
conclusion of the de-energization event.
When SDG&E considers calling, sustaining, or curtailing de-energization events, detailed 
analysis is conducted to determine critical wildfire conditions are occurring across the 
landscape.  SDG&E leverages its situational awareness tools, including the weather station 
network.  SDG&E also conducts a detailed analysis of the Fire Potential Index to determine 
the risk that a wildfire will grow rapidly, should an ignition occur.  SDG&E’s FPI indicated 
that large fires were possible should an ignition occur.  The qualitative and quantitative

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-9
factors considered in the FPI determining the fire environment was critically dry are further 
discussed below. 
SDG&E leverages satellite data to closely monitor the greenness of the grass across its 
service territory.  As demonstrated in the graph below, following early season rainfall and 
some greening of the annual grasses, satellites were confirming visual observations that there 
had been a decline in greenness of the annual grasses, increasing wildfire potential.  
Figure 6: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) measured weekly from low 
earth orbiting satellites at a resolution of 3.7m for 20 grassland areas in San Diego 
County 
In addition to the drying of the annual grasses, SDG&E has also been measuring and 
observing a significant drying of the dead fuel moistures across the region this year.  This 
drying of the dead fuels is demonstrated in the graph below of Energy Release Component 
(ERC), which is an indicator of the intensity by which a wildfire could burn.  As noted in the 
graph below, due to recent hot and dry weather, the ERCs across our region were reaching 
near record levels for that date, further supporting the potential for a large and destructive 
wildfire, should an ignition occur.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
 
A-10 
Figure 7: Dead Fuel Moistures 
 
Live Fuel Moisture is also closely monitored, measured and analyzed when considering 
PSPS.  The graph below demonstrates the Live Fuel Moisture reading that was incorporated 
in the Fire Potential Index.  As shown, Live Fuel Moisture, which is an indication of the 
moisture content of the living vegetation was below average and below critical levels, further 
exacerbating the wildfire risk.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
 
A-11 
Figure 8: Live Fuel Moistures 
 
Over the past year, SDG&E has developed more granular modeling of the probability of 
ignition and probability of failure at the asset and ignition source level. During this PSPS 
event, SDG&E incorporated the new real time risk assessment model called the Wildfire 
Next Generation System – Operations model (WiNGS-Ops) to evaluate and compare 
Wildfire and PSPS risks at the asset level (pole/span), as well as at the sub-circuit/segment 
level. Since this is a new model, the output of WiNGS-Ops was used as an additional data 
point to help inform the decision makers, but it was not fully embedded in the PSPS decision 
making. The model takes into account the probability of failure, probability of ignition and 
the consequence of a risk event at each pole and span location, as a function of wind.  
SDG&E plans to continue to evaluate and enhance WiNGS-Ops with development of more 
granular machine learning probability of failure, probability of ignition, consequence models 
for different assets and failure modes and continue to enhance PSPS models.  
 
This information above was coupled with a forecast of strong and potentially damaging 
winds to determine that the conditions could become unsafe, which led to the initiation of the 
PSPS event.  As the weather event began, wind gusts were monitored closely in real-time.  
As discussed in section 5 below, PSPS was considered and, in certain instances implemented, 
in real-time once alert speeds were reached.  In sum, SDG&E’s analytical tools and 
operational experience supported initiation of PSPS events at certain locations as a measure 
of last resort to avoid the risk of catastrophic wildfires.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-12
4. An explanation of how the utility determined that the benefit of de-energization
outweighed potential public safety risks, and analysis of the risks of de-energization
against not de-energizing. The utility must identify and quantify customer, resident,
and the general public risks and harms from de-energization and clearly explain risk
models, risk assessment processes, and provide further documentation on how the
power disruptions to customers, residents, and the general public is weighed against the
benefits of a proactive de-energization.
To determine whether the benefit of de-energization (PSPS) outweighed the potential public 
safety risks, SDG&E modeled the opposing scenarios in accordance with the risk 
quantification framework reported in the 2021 RAMP filing, which uses a multi-attribute 
value function (MAVF) to quantify risk. Based on probabilistic modeling and a set of 
assumptions, SDG&E identified wind speeds for which de-energization would likely produce 
a favorable outcome to customers and the public. This analysis was performed for each 
segment with the potential for PSPS and reported in Table 2 for segments that were 
ultimately de-energized during this event. In the days leading up to the event, SDG&E used 
wind forecasts to identify high-risk segments to carefully monitor.  
The risk quantifications consider the expected value of the risks for each scenario and 
segment. For the non-PSPS scenario, this is the probability of ignition from the assets on the 
segment multiplied by the quantified consequence of that wildfire. For the PSPS scenario, it 
is only the quantified risk of de-energization, since the event has a one hundred percent 
probability when it is initialized by SDG&E. In the iteration of the models used for this 
event, only the probability of ignition varies with wind gust. 
To quantify the consequence of PSPS and wildfire, SDG&E used models to estimate the top-
level attributes that comprise the MAVF: safety, reliability, financial, and stakeholder 
satisfaction. The models for PSPS consequence are simplistic but require some considerable 
assumptions described in the tables below. For wildfire consequence, SDG&E used the fire 
spread models developed by Technosylva, Inc, which was described in SDG&E’s 2021 
WMP filing. The Technosylva models output fire consequence in units not directly relatable 
to the MAVF core attributes, such as structures impacted, population impacted, and acres 
burned. Therefore, an additional layer of assumptions is required to “convert” the 
Technosylva model outputs to MAVF values. The calculation methodologies are reported in 
the Figure 9. The resulting wildfire consequence values for each device that was de-
energized is shown in Table 2.

In addition to the uncertainty of the model assumptions, the model methodologies themselves 
are continually improving. The models used for this event were first introduced this year, and 
therefore may be missing some key factors driving the decision to de-energize. Therefore, 
some discretion is necessary when weighing these model outputs against other observations.

A-14
Future iterations of these models are expected to prove more accurate, reliable, and all-
encompassing. For this event, some reasons for de-energizing at wind speeds differing from 
the model outputs are: 
−
Non-standard, temporary configuration
−
Shorter PSPS duration
−
Longer decision interval (not hourly)
−
Updated ground information
−
Low customer count
−
Weather station proximity
5. Explanation of alternatives considered and evaluation of each alternative.
Prior to and during the event, SDG&E considered alternatives to PSPS by considering 
various factors. These included weather information to understand the scope of the PSPS 
event, initiating patrols prior to event to understand the field conditions and the grid 
conditions, assessing temporary construction configurations and asset management 
inspection conditions, reviewing the vegetation risk index data, reviewing the conductor risk 
data, and monitoring 30 second weather station reads to ensure wind alert speeds would 
indeed pose enough of a wildfire risk prior to triggering PSPS. Additionally, SDG&E looks 
for opportunities to cutover segments of circuits which may be less impacted by the 
forecasted weather to other circuits if the feed to these segments is from a circuit that may be 
affected by PSPS.  
•
Weather analysis prior to the PSPS event. As described above, weather related
information (enhanced with AI forecasting) informs SDG&E’s PSPS operations,
providing a better understanding of the potential scope of circuit segments impacted.
Utilizing the weather forecast, SDG&E further narrows the list of forecasted circuit
segments as the event gets closer.
•
Patrols prior to the event. Patrols conducted prior to the event inform the PSPS
decision-making process.  If any unmitigable conditions are found during the patrols,
it could potentially lead to PSPS. Patrols also provide an alternative to PSPS and keep
the power on for areas found to be clear as long as no other conditions point to a
wildfire risk.
•
Temporary configurations and asset conditions. Prior to an event, an assessment of
any ongoing construction and temporary conditions of the grid are identified to factor
these known conditions into a decision for PSPS. The Corrective Maintenance
Program (CMP) is also leveraged to understand any outstanding maintenance
conditions of grid assets.
•
Circuit Risk Index (CRI). CRI is probabilistic model that evaluates the risk of wind-
driven conductor failure and ignition on a given segment. For example, segments with
more small copper wires are flagged as higher risk than other segments that have
thicker newer wire installed via hardening programs. SDG&E uses this information to
determine whether a circuit segment has small wire associated with high failure rate
under high wind conditions, which plays a part in determining the level of wildfire
risk.
•
30 second weather station reads during the event. The 30 second reads from
weather stations provide the wind gusts and duration associated with each weather
station. This read informs SDG&E as to how close the wind speeds are to the alert

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff Post-Event Report: November 24 – November 26, 2021 
A-15
speeds for which PSPS consideration may be triggered. Many circuit segments were 
not de-energized based on the 30 second read information. 
During the post event analysis of this event, SDG&E determined that there were 58 
sectionalizing devices identified in which the wind speeds met the pre-determined alert speed 
prior to the event, but real-time considerations during the event supported decisions to not 
initiate a PSPS for these devices.  Approximately 25,000 customers were located in these 
areas where a PSPS was avoided.  Some considerations that were included in keeping 
customers energized included: 
•
30-second weather reading indicated that strong wind gusts were short lived and not
persistent.
•
The Fire Potential Index was indicating that conditions were not “Extreme” in the
area, including SME input on rainfall earlier in the season.
•
SMEs were advising that wind speeds were near peak and not expected to rise further.
•
Winds were occurring in areas prone to strong winds.
•
The electric system was performing well and faults were not observed in the area of
the higher winds.
•
There was minimal wildfire activity being reported across the region.
Section 3 – De-energized Time, Place, Duration and Customers

applicable.
The PSPS event began on 11/24/21 at 11:47 and concluded 11/26/21 at 16:37 with a total
duration of 52 hours and 50 minutes.  The event was located in portions of San Diego
County.  During the event, the majority of patrol and restoration activities occurred on
11/26/21, but some limited patrols and restorations occurred on 11/25/21, as conditions
warranted.

Section 8 – Power Restoration 
 
1. A detailed explanation of the steps the utility took to restore power. 
 
When a circuit is de-energized, meteorology will add it to the restoration forecast list, and the 
team will ascertain the date and time when forecasted wind gusts are expected to reach 7mph 
less than the alert speed and will likely continue to decline.  As circuits are de-energized, 
they are added to the dynamic restoration forecast list.  Circuit restoration is prioritized based 
on the order in which favorable weather conditions will prevail in each area.  Forecasts 
trending in a favorable manner will garner the prioritization of patrols.  Once the patrolling of 
the lines is complete, the circuit will be re-energized knowing that favorable weather is in the 
forecast for that circuit.

1. Mitigation actions and impacts (both waterfall graph and map) including: 
sectionalization devices, temporary generation, microgrids, permanent backup

SDG&E implements mitigation measures used to decrease the risk of utility caused wildfires 
by reinforcing the standards listed in SDG&E Electric Standard Practice 113.1—Operations 
and Maintenance Wildland Fire Prevention Plan and increasing use of prevention resources. 
All SDG&E field personnel are required to receive annual training on fire prevention. All 
non-emergency work is restricted in areas where there is extreme fire potential.

Sectionalizing Devices: 
SDG&E utilized sectionalization during this weather event to reduce PSPS customer impacts. 
Leveraging real-time data from the SDG&E weather network in the area of the severe 
weather, SDG&E was able to confirm the strong winds were isolated to portions of the 
majority of impacted circuits. As a result, SDG&E de-energized only portions of 10 out of 13 
circuits impacted during this weather event, as opposed to entire circuits. By de-energizing 
only portions of the circuits, SDG&E was able to avert PSPS impacts for approximately 
7,956 customer accounts.

Temporary Generation: 
As part of its Generator Grant Program, SDG&E has offered portable backup battery units 
(e.g., Goal Zero Yeti 3000) to MBL customers who live in the HFTD and have been 
impacted by PSPS in previous years. As of December 2021, SDG&E has provided more than 
3,689 backup batteries since the start of the program in 2019. 
 
In addition, SDG&E has completed the installation of 390 generators as part of the Fixed 
Backup Power Program (formerly the Whole Home Generator Program), providing those 
customers the option to remain energized during the PSPS event. In support of this program, 
SDG&E’s team deployed two portable, conventional generators at the Barrett Mobile Home 
Park in Dulzura and at the Heavenly Oaks Mobile Home Park in Descanso.  Ultimately, there 
were no outages on these circuits, and the generators were not engaged. 
 
Microgrids: 
SDG&E successfully established temporary configurations for microgrids at the following 
locations: Julian, Butterfield Ranch, Shelter Valley, and Cameron Corners. For this event, 
only Butterfield Ranch and Shelter Valley were engaged while Julian and Cameron Corners 
were on stand-by. While these customers are included in the customer count impacted by de-
energizations provided in response to Question #3 above, the customer counts provided 
below still received electricity from SDG&E through the microgrid configurations and did 
not suffer loss of power as a result of the PSPS events listed in this post-event report.

Permanent Backup Generation 
SDG&E currently has two projects nearing completion for permanent backup generation: 
Cameron Corners and Ramona Air Attack Base. Once complete, these sites will be 100% 
renewable-based microgrids. 
 
Transmission Switching: 
SDG&E did not utilize any transmission switching for this event. TL634 was on the list for 
potential transmission switching, but after further investigation into the TL alert speed and 
the expected forecast, SDG&E determined that it was not necessary to switch. SDG&E grid 
control coordinated pre-event with the Imperial Irrigation District to prepare to switch in 
TL800, which would allow us to restore 2,766 customers at Borrego if needed. 
 
Other Grid Hardening: 
Hellhole Canyon weather station reported a peak of 61 mph winds during the early morning 
hours of 11/25.  This value would have historically resulted in sectionalizing device C1030-
987 being de-energized and 31 customers being without power.  As a result of 
undergrounding the distribution electrical system around this weather station, SDG&E 
avoided de-energizing these customers for this event. Historically, this section of circuit 1030

1. Threshold analysis and the results of the utility’s examination of whether its thresholds 
are adequate and correctly applied in the de-energized areas.  
 
SDG&E believes its thresholds for de-energizing during this event were adequate. SDG&E 
will continue to monitor its performance throughout the season to determine whether changes 
to its thresholds are warranted. Such changes require more time to evaluate because they 
could involve updates to models, testing of those updates and stakeholder engagement to 
institute those changes.

SDG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff possible in 24-48 hours.
This is an important safety message from SDG&E. This information is intended for public safety and government 
partners. Please do not share this message publicly. Please use the social media kit and community flyer provided 
below to share with your communities. 
The National Weather Service today upgraded the Fire Weather Watch to a Red Flag Warning, to be in effect from 
Thursday, November 25 at 4 a.m., through Friday, November 26 at 6 p.m. for the San Diego County valleys and 
mountains. Strong gusty Santa Ana winds and low humidity are forecast through Saturday. The winds are forecast to 
peak on Thursday morning with gusts 40 - 60 mph. 
SDG&E plans to activate its Emergency Operations Center to monitor high fire risk weather conditions which may force 
SDG&E to shut off power to reduce the risk of wildfire. The estimated start time of event is 6 p.m. on Wednesday, 
November 24. We anticipate the event could last until Saturday, November 27, with full restoration by approximately 6 
p.m.

Date:
Monday, November 22, 2021 4:59:37 PM
Hello,
 
Today, November 22, 2021, SDG&E initiated its Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS)
protocols based on Santa Ana weather conditions and a Fire Weather Watch issued by the
National Weather Service forecasted to impact San Diego County starting on Wednesday,
November 24, 2021. SDG&E has not activated its Emergency Operations Center (EOC).
SDG&E’s EOC staff will remain in a monitoring and planning mode until further notice.
 
At this time, SDG&E expects to provide advanced notification to 28,664 customer accounts
that will potentially be impacted by this event, including 2,229 MBL customers. All of the
potentially impacted areas are located within Tier 2 and 3 of the HFTD. Additional
information, including anticipating timing of de-energization and re-energization,
consolidated device information, maps, and GIS shapefiles are available on SDG&E’s secure
PSPS partner portal at https://portal.sdgepartners.com.
 
Weather event details
Santa Ana weather conditions are expected to arrive in SDG&E’s service area on
Wednesday, November 24. Winds are expected to peak in the morning on Thursday,
November 25 and gradually decrease by Friday evening.
Fire Potential Index (FPI) on Thursday through Saturday expected to be elevated in all
of San Diego County and in Southern Orange County.
 
Unless there are changes requiring immediate notification, we will provide another update
tomorrow, Tuesday, November 23.
 
Thank you,
SDG&E Regulatory Affairs

Issue
Discussion
Resolution
Many new EOC responders 
The EOC has an annual 40% attrition rate which has a high training burden.  
With the virtual environment, it is challenging to effectively train 
responders from 35 business units throughout the company many who 
have never had an emergency response role.
Diversify training methodologies and 
delivery modalities. 
Manual Data entry
The CalOES PowerPoint requires extensive manual data entry from 
multiple business units.
Resolution is pending.
Public Safety Partner 
notification system had a 
category flagging issue with 
22 contacts
22 contacts were not coded appropriately in the system which affected 
their notifications.
They have all been recoded and category has 
been deleted.
AFN Support Partner: Warm 
Food
Caterers contracted to supply food support for warm meals were closed 
for Thanksgiving holiday and did not have staffing support or food 
inventory supply to support food requested.
Logistics and supplier diversity teams were 
able to assist with vendors for this PSPS.
Warm food contracts and availability 
confirmation earlier in event to allow for 
alternatives if needed.
Customer Notifications 
received as “Spam” calls
SDG&E received feedback from customers that notification calls are being 
flagged as spam calls, so they are not answering them and we do not have 
the ability to leave a voicemail on a rejected call.
SDG&E will meet with telecoms to 
determine how to ensure emergency calls 
are not flagged as Spam.
